title: Signing Up on Render with GitHub: What It Actually Does
excerpt: Why connecting GitHub during Render's sign-up flow saves you a step, what the authorization is actually granting, and how to get an account set up without extra friction.

content.text: When I needed a place to host a small Node.js API for testing, I didn't want to deal with setting up servers, configuring Nginx, or managing SSH keys just to see if the project worked. That's basically why Render exists, and why so many people recommend it for small to mid-sized projects.
In this post I want to go through:

items: What Render actually is
Why signing up with GitHub makes sense
What that authorization is actually granting
How to create the account, step by step

content.text: What is Render?

Render is a cloud hosting platform. You give it a Git repository, and it builds and runs your app for you. You don't touch a Linux server directly. No manually installing Node, no configuring a reverse proxy, no setting up a process manager like PM2.
Render supports a few different things:

items: Web services (this is what you'd use for a Node.js API)
Static sites (for frontend builds like a React app)
Background workers
Cron jobs
Managed PostgreSQL and Redis (called Key Value on Render)

content.text: For a Node.js backend, "web service" is the one you want — more on actually deploying one in a follow-up post.
Why Sign Up with GitHub Instead of Email

Render lets you sign up with GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Google, or a plain email and password. Technically, all of them work. But if your project already lives on GitHub, connecting through GitHub saves you an extra step later.

Here's the thing I didn't realize at first: connecting GitHub for **login** and connecting GitHub for **deployment** are two separate things on Render. You can log in with email and still connect GitHub later just to pull your repos, or you can do both through GitHub in one go.
If you sign up with GitHub directly, Render authorizes access to your GitHub account as part of the sign-up flow. That means:

items: You skip creating a separate password for Render.
Your GitHub repos show up right away when you go to create a service.
Every time you push new code to your connected branch, Render can automatically rebuild and redeploy it, without you doing anything manually.

content.text: If you sign up with plain email instead, you'll still need to connect GitHub afterward from your account settings before you can deploy anything from a repo. So functionally, signing up with GitHub is just doing that step upfront instead of doing it twice.

One thing worth knowing: if you connect GitHub for login, and you have an existing Render account tied to the same email as your GitHub account, Render will just log you into that existing account instead of creating a new one. So it's not going to create duplicate accounts by accident.

content.alt: Flow diagram showing four steps: click sign up with GitHub, authorize on GitHub, get redirected to the dashboard, repos are ready to deploy
content.caption: One authorization on GitHub is all it takes to link your repos to Render.

content.text: Creating the Account

If you don't already have a GitHub account, you'll need one first. On github.com, click **Sign up**, enter an email, create a password, pick a username, and verify your email address. That part is separate from Render entirely.
Once GitHub is sorted, go to render.com and:

items: Click **Get Started** (or **Sign Up**).
Choose **GitHub** as the sign-up method.

GitHub will ask you to authorize Render to access your account. You can allow access to all repositories or only specific ones. I'd recommend picking specific repos if you're cautious about what you give a third-party platform access to, though most tutorials just select all.
You'll be redirected back to the Render dashboard, and your GitHub repos should now be visible when you create a new service.

content.text: That's really it. No credit card required to sign up or to deploy something on the free tier. With the account connected, the next step is actually deploying something — I cover deploying a Node.js app as a web service, plus the free-tier trade-offs, in a separate post.

title: Deploying a Node.js App on Render (and the Free-Tier Trade-offs)
excerpt: How to actually deploy a Node.js API as a Render web service, the PORT gotcha that makes healthy deploys look broken, and the free-tier trade-offs that catch people off guard later.

content.text: Once your Render account is connected to GitHub, the actual deploy is the easy part. This post walks through deploying a Node.js API as a web service, then goes into the trade-offs of Render's free tier — the part a lot of beginner guides skip.
Deploying a Node.js Project as a Web Service
Assuming your Node.js project is already pushed to a GitHub repo, here's the general flow:

content.alt: Flow diagram showing four steps: push to GitHub, Render build, start command, then a live URL
content.caption: Push to your branch and Render takes it from there — build, start, live.

items: From the Render dashboard, click **New** and select **Web Service**.
Pick the GitHub repository you want to deploy. If you don't see it listed, you may need to click "Configure account" and grant Render access to that specific repo.

items.text: Render will try to detect your project automatically. For a typical Node.js app, it usually suggests:
sublist: **Build Command**: `npm install` (or `npm ci` if you have a lock file and want a cleaner install)
**Start Command**: `node index.js` or `npm start`, depending on your `package.json`

items: Choose an instance type. The **Free** tier works fine for testing.
Add any environment variables your app needs (database URL, API keys, `PORT`, etc.) under the Environment section.
Click **Create Web Service**.

content.text: Render will pull your repo, run the build command, then start your app. You can watch the logs in real time while it deploys.
A couple of practical notes I'd flag here, since they trip people up:
Your app needs to listen on the port Render provides through the `PORT` environment variable, not a hardcoded port like `3000`. Something like:

content.code:
const PORT = process.env.PORT || 3000;
app.listen(PORT, () => console.log(`Server running on port ${PORT}`));

content.text: If you hardcode the port instead of reading it from `process.env.PORT`, Render's health checks won't be able to reach your app, and the deploy will look like it failed even though your code is fine.
Every time you push to the connected branch (usually `main`), Render automatically triggers a new build and deploy. You don't need to log in and redeploy manually.
Why You'd Want to Deploy a Node.js App on Render

**It's genuinely fast to get something live.** For a side project or a demo you want to share quickly, you can go from "code on GitHub" to "live URL" in a few minutes, without touching server configuration.
**Automatic deploys from Git.** Once it's connected, pushing to your branch is basically your deploy pipeline. You don't need to set up your own CI/CD just for a simple deploy.
**Free tier exists without a credit card.** That matters for students, portfolio projects, and anything you're not sure will need to run long-term.
**Managed databases are available too.** If your Node app needs PostgreSQL or Redis, Render can host those alongside your service, so you're not juggling multiple providers for a small project.
Why You Might Not Want To (The Trade-offs)
This is the part a lot of beginner guides skip, and it's where I'd push back a little on always recommending Render without context.

content.alt: Diagram of the free-tier spin-down cycle: active, then asleep after idle time, then a cold start, then active again
content.caption: The free-tier reality: idle for ~15 minutes, then a 30–60 second cold start on the next request.

content.text: **Free web services spin down after inactivity.** As of what I found researching this, Render's free instances go to sleep after about 15 minutes without incoming traffic, and the next request after that can take something like 30 to 60 seconds while it spins back up. For a personal API or demo, that's usually fine. For anything where someone is waiting on a response in real time — like a production API, a webhook receiver, or anything time-sensitive — that cold start is a real problem.

**Free tier is not meant for production traffic.** The free plan gives you limited RAM and CPU (from what I saw, around 512 MB RAM and a fraction of a CPU core). That's enough for testing and small side projects, not for something with real, sustained traffic.

**Costs can add up as you scale.** Moving to an always-on instance starts at a small monthly fee, but once you add a production-grade database, more RAM, or higher bandwidth, the total cost climbs. A few comparisons I came across mentioned that at high traffic volumes, Render can end up more expensive than some usage-based alternatives like Railway or Fly.io, mainly because Render's pricing model isn't purely usage-based like theirs.

**Free databases expire.** Free PostgreSQL instances on Render have a fixed storage limit and get deleted automatically after a set number of days unless you upgrade. This is easy to forget if you're using the free database for something you actually care about keeping.
What I'd Take Away From This
For learning, prototyping, or showing a recruiter a working project, Render is a solid, low-friction option to deploy to once your GitHub account is connected.

Where I'd be more careful is assuming the free tier behaves like a "real" hosting setup. The spin-down behavior and the database expiry aren't hidden, but they're easy to miss until your app goes to sleep in the middle of a demo. If a project moves past the "just testing it" stage, it's worth deciding early whether you actually need an always-on instance, rather than finding out the hard way when someone hits your sleeping API and waits a full minute for a response.

title: Keeping a Render Free Web Service Awake with UptimeRobot
excerpt: How UptimeRobot's monitoring pings double as a way to stop a free Render web service from spinning down, how the monitoring itself actually works, and where this workaround falls short.

content.text: In an earlier post I went over why Render's free web services spin down after about 15 minutes of no traffic, and why the cold start on the next request can take 30 to 60 seconds. The most common fix people reach for is UptimeRobot: point a free monitor at your service, and the periodic checks keep it from ever going idle long enough to sleep. It works, but it's worth understanding what UptimeRobot is actually doing before relying on it.
In this post:

items: What UptimeRobot is and who it's really built for
How its monitoring checks actually work
How to point one at a Render service, step by step
What the free plan does and doesn't give you
Whether this genuinely solves the free-tier problem

content.text: What Is UptimeRobot?

UptimeRobot is an uptime monitoring service. You give it a URL, and it checks that URL on a schedule from its own servers, then alerts you if the check starts failing. It's built for the opposite problem to the one we're using it for here — its actual job is telling you when something you host **goes down**, not keeping something artificially up.

That side-effect is why it's become the go-to trick for Render's free tier: a monitoring check is, functionally, just an HTTP request. If that request lands on your Render service often enough, Render never sees the service go quiet, so it never spins it down.
How UptimeRobot Actually Works

When you create an HTTP(s) monitor, UptimeRobot sends a request to your URL at whatever interval you set and records the response. If it gets back a healthy status code within a reasonable time, the check passes. If a request times out or comes back with an error status, UptimeRobot doesn't immediately mark you as down — it retries, and only flags the monitor as **down** after a small number of consecutive failures, so a single slow response doesn't trigger a false alarm.

Every check gets logged, which is how it builds the uptime percentage and response-time history you see on the dashboard. If you've set up alert contacts, a status change (up to down, or down back to up) triggers a notification by email, browser push, or a webhook, depending on what you've configured.

content.alt: Flow diagram showing four steps: UptimeRobot pings the URL, Render receives a request, the 15-minute idle timer resets, and the service stays awake
content.caption: The monitoring check and the keep-alive effect are the same HTTP request — UptimeRobot doesn't know it's doing the second thing.

content.text: None of this is Render-specific. UptimeRobot has no idea your target happens to spin down when idle — it's just doing its normal job of checking a URL on a schedule. The keep-alive effect is a byproduct of the check interval being shorter than Render's idle window, not a feature either service advertises together.
Setting Up a Monitor for Your Render Service
Assuming your service is already deployed and live at something like `yourapp.onrender.com`:

items: Create a free account at uptimerobot.com.
From the dashboard, click **Add New Monitor**.
Set **Monitor Type** to **HTTP(s)**.
Give it a **Friendly Name** so you can recognize it later.

items.text: For the **URL**, point it at a lightweight route rather than your homepage:
sublist: A dedicated health-check endpoint is ideal, since it doesn't touch a database or do any real work.
Hitting a heavier page every 5 minutes just to trigger a response works too, but it's doing more than necessary for a check that only needs a 200.

items: Set **Monitoring Interval** to 5 minutes — that's the minimum the free plan allows, and it's well inside Render's ~15-minute idle window.
Add an alert contact (your email is fine) so you actually hear about it if the service goes down for a real reason.
Click **Create Monitor**.

content.text: If you don't already have a simple health route, something like this in an Express app is enough:

That's genuinely the whole setup. Within a few minutes you'll see the first checks come in on the dashboard, and as long as they keep landing every 5 minutes, your service shouldn't spin down between them.
UptimeRobot's Free Plan Limits
The free plan is generous enough for this use case, but it's worth knowing the boundaries:

items: Up to 50 monitors, which is far more than a single side project needs.
5-minute checks is the shortest interval available — 1-minute checks are a paid feature.
Covers HTTP(s), keyword, ping, and port monitor types, not just plain uptime checks.
Alerting covers email and browser push by default, with some webhook and integration options.
Log history is kept, but the retention window is limited compared to paid plans.

content.alt: Terminal-style panel listing UptimeRobot's free plan limits: 50 monitors, 5-minute minimum interval, and basic alert channels
content.caption: 5 minutes is as fast as the free plan checks — which happens to be exactly fast enough for this trick.

content.text: Does This Actually Solve the Free-Tier Problem?
Partially, and it's worth being honest about the parts it doesn't fix.

**Render's free plan still has a monthly instance-hour budget.** From what I found researching this, free web services share a pool of 750 instance hours per month across your account. A 30-day month is 720 hours, so that budget comfortably covers one service running the entire month without a single spin-down. That's the actual math behind this trick: 750 free hours, 720 hours in the month, which means one account can technically keep one free service pinged by UptimeRobot and running non-stop, all month, and still not hit the cap. Try to do that with a second free service at the same time, though, and you're well past 750 combined hours before the month is out — Render pauses whichever service pushes you over, regardless of how often UptimeRobot is pinging it.

**It's a workaround, not a guarantee.** The check only needs to land before Render's idle window closes, which normally isn't an issue at a 5-minute interval — but if UptimeRobot has an outage of its own, or the monitor gets misconfigured, you can still get a cold start on the next real visitor.

**It's not really what the free tier is for.** Render's free instances are meant for testing and low-traffic projects that can tolerate spinning down between uses. Keeping one artificially always-on gets you closer to production behavior without paying for it, but for anything where uptime actually matters, the more honest fix is paying for an always-on instance rather than engineering around the free one.
What I'd Take Away From This

For a portfolio API, a demo you link in a resume, or a side project you don't want to explain a 45-second delay for, an UptimeRobot monitor pointed at a `/health` route is a genuinely useful five-minute setup. It's free, it's simple, and it also gives you actual downtime alerts as a side benefit.
Just don't mistake it for the same thing as an always-on production instance. It's a way to make the free tier behave better within its own limits, not a way to bypass those limits entirely.
